hook_text: Your brain is filling in a hole in your vision right now.
You can't tickle yourself. Your brain predicts the touch before it lands.
Your brain hides a blur every time your eyes jump.
Every time you recall a memory, your brain can quietly change it.
Right now your brain is ignoring the feeling of your socks.
Your brain judges a face in a fraction of a second.
Your brain treats a stranger's confidence like proof. It isn't.
In a loud room, your brain still catches your own name.
Your brain may remember unfinished tasks longer. Or so the theory says.
Your brain thinks a long line means a better restaurant.
Your brain sees motion in this still picture. Nothing is moving.
Your brain makes a loss sting more than the same gain feels good.
Your brain notices bad news faster than good news.
Your brain may replay what you learned today while you sleep.
Your brain fills the gaps in a story with details that never happened.
Say the color of each word, not the word itself. Go.
Close one eye and stare at the cross. The dot will vanish.
Read this list once. In ten seconds I'll ask what was in it.
Stare at the dot for twenty seconds, then look at a white wall.
Which line is longer? Answer before the arrows disappear.
Count the passes the white team makes. Don't miss one.
Spot what changes between these two pictures. Take your time.
Watch the mouth and listen. Now close your eyes. Did the sound change?
Try to remember these seven digits without writing them down.
Look at this outlet. Do you see a face? You're not alone.
Guess: is the population of this city above or below this number?
Rate this face in half a second. Trustworthy or not?
Picture a cheap, a mid-price and a pricey popcorn. Which do you pick?
Say 'silk' five times fast. Now, what do cows drink?
Try to remember a dream from last night. How much is left?
In 1951, a psychologist asked people to judge which line was longest.
In 1963, volunteers were told to give shocks. The shocks weren't real.
In 1971, students were split into guards and prisoners in a basement.
In 1961, kids watched an adult punch a doll. Then they played.
In 1974, people watched a car crash film. One word changed their memory.
In 1885, one man memorized nonsense syllables to measure forgetting.
In 1953, researchers noticed sleepers' eyes darting under their eyelids.
In 1968, students heard someone seem to have a seizure. Who helped?
In 1959, students were paid to lie about a boring task.
In 1999, about half of viewers counting passes missed a gorilla suit.
In 1960, students tried to find the rule behind 2, 4, 6.
In 1924, two psychologists tested memory after sleep versus after a day awake.
In 1974, researchers spun a wheel of fortune before asking a simple question.
Over a century ago, an engineer measured how hard teams pulled a rope.
In 1979, psychologists asked people to choose between a sure loss and a gamble.
You keep watching a bad movie because you paid for the ticket. Name it.
After the game, you 'knew it all along.' What's that called?
You only notice news that proves you right. Name that bias.
You think everyone noticed your stain. Almost nobody did. Name it.
One good trait makes you assume a person is good at everything. Name it.
Plane crashes feel more common than they are. What's that bias?
They cut you off: rude. You cut them off: bad day. Name it.
You value your old mug more just because it's yours. Name it.
A medium popcorn priced near the large makes the large look smart. Name it.
The worst scorers rated themselves above average. Name the effect.
Everyone in the group slacks a little when the work is shared. Name it.
A song you disliked grows on you after a few plays. Name it.
You recall a list's first and last items best. What's that called?
Everyone in the room agrees, so you change your answer. Name it.
You pick the default option on every form without reading. Name it.
Why do you forget why you walked into a room?
Why a word sits on the tip of your tongue and won't come out.
Why you hear your own name across a noisy party.
Why dreams fade so fast after you wake up.
Why you see faces in clouds, cars and power outlets.
Why cramming the night before feels like it works, but doesn't last.
Why you keep paying for the gym you never use.
Why you feel awkward hours after a tiny mistake.
Why one bad review sticks with you more than ten good ones.
Why you remember the end of a vacation more than the middle.
Why you feel sleepy in the afternoon even after a good night.
Why you can't stop thinking about a show that ended on a cliffhanger.
Why you go along with the group even when you disagree.
Why the person who names a number first sets the price.
Why familiar faces start to feel friendlier over time.
You've heard willpower runs out like fuel. Big repeat studies found almost nothing.
Power poses were said to change your hormones. Repeat studies didn't find that.
The famous pen-in-teeth smile study? A 17-lab repeat found no effect.
Reading words about old age made people walk slower. Later labs couldn't repeat it.
Thinking about professors to ace a quiz? That priming effect didn't replicate.
The marshmallow test predicted less than you were told.
Too many jam choices stop shoppers buying? Later studies found mixed results.
Holding a warm drink makes you judge people warmer? Repeat studies struggled.
Washing your hands to ease guilt? Repeat studies mostly didn't find it.
Pictures of eyes make people more honest? Bigger studies found the effect shaky.
A sugary drink restores willpower? Later work found that claim weak.
A 2011 study claimed people sensed the future. Repeat attempts found nothing.
Seeing red makes you score worse on tests? Retests found much weaker effects.
Playing Mozart won't make babies smarter. The original study tested college students.
The Stanford prison experiment is famous. Its conclusions are heavily disputed now.
You walked into the kitchen and forgot why. The doorway may be to blame.
Your clearest memory of a big day may be the least accurate.
One word in a question can change what witnesses remember.
You can remember an event that never happened. Labs have shown it.
Try drawing a coin from memory. People get it wrong surprisingly often.
You reread your notes three times and still blanked. Here's a better way.
You'd swear you said it. Your friend swears they did.
You remember the gist of a list, plus a word that wasn't there.
Seven is the famous memory limit. The real number may be smaller.
You remember a dream for seconds, then it's gone.
Your memory of a song's lyrics can be confidently wrong.
A night of sleep can help a new memory stick.
You forget much of what you learn within days, unless you review it.
Few people remember anything before age three. It has a name.
You can forget a name while remembering their job, hobbies and dog.
There's a name for seeing faces in things that aren't faces.
There's a word for a song stuck in your head on repeat.
There's a name for waking up unable to move for a few seconds.
There's a word for knowing you're dreaming while you dream.
There's a name for forgetting why you entered a room.
There's a name for the jolt you feel just as you fall asleep.
There's a word for liking something just because it's familiar.
There's a name for thinking you knew it all along.
There's a name for doing less work when you're in a group.
There's a word for the sleepy dip you feel after lunch.
There's a name for not seeing something right in front of you.
There's a name for remembering the start and the end, but not the middle.
There's a name for judging an experience by its peak and its end.
There's a word for a feeling of 'I've lived this moment before.'
There's a name for a sound that changes when you watch the lips.
You've heard we only use 10% of our brains. Brain scans disagree.
You've heard you're either left-brained or right-brained. Brain scans don't show it.
You've heard you learn best in your 'learning style.' Tests don't back it.
You've heard humans now have shorter attention spans than goldfish. There's no good source.
You've heard punching a pillow lets your anger out. Studies say it doesn't.
You've heard opposites attract. Research mostly finds similar people pair up.
You've heard listening to classical music makes you smarter. Not quite.
You've heard habits take 21 days. One study found it often took much longer.
You've heard lie detectors catch liars. Scientists say they're not reliable.
You've heard eyes looking up-left mean someone's lying. Tests found nothing.
You've heard dreams last only a few seconds. Lab studies suggest otherwise.
You've heard you can learn a language in your sleep. Not really.
You've heard memory works like a video camera. It doesn't.
You've heard sugar makes kids hyper. Blind studies didn't find that.
You've heard the full moon makes people act strange. Data says no.
Would you give the wrong answer if everyone else did?
Would you rather a sure win or a coin flip for double?
Would you help a stranger if five other people were watching?
Would you eat one treat now or wait for two later?
Would you swap your mug for a chocolate bar? Many people won't.
Would you sign up as an organ donor if the box were pre-ticked?
Would a pricier option on the menu make you spend more?
Would you save 200 people for sure, or gamble on saving all 600?
Would you rather have a cold-water test end gently or end sooner?
Would you notice if the person you were talking to was swapped?
Would you change your answer if a confident person disagreed?
Would you rather choose from six jams or twenty-four?
Would you lie about a boring task for a tiny payment?
Would you work as hard on a team as you would alone?
Would you sleep on a hard problem or keep working through the night?
